speechtext:
May
I direct a question to the Minister of National Defence, notice of which I have sent him. Has the minister's attention been called to an article in the Vancouver Sun, alleging that goods are being smuggled into Canada from the Far East through the army mails? Can the minister also say what exemptions from customs duties are granted to service personnel?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: ALLEGED SMUGGLING FROM FAR EAST THROUGH ARMY MAILS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. The hon. member for
50433-236J
Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) also gave me notice of a similar question. I have seen a copy of the rather, to me at least, astonishing article to which the hon. member has referred.
In reply, I would like to say that it has been our policy to investigate immediately and thoroughly any report of alleged irregularities of whatever kind, and from whatever source, even though, as I indicated to the house in the answer which I made to a question on April 18, many of these reports are later found to be either without foundation or greatly exaggerated.
With regard to the specific matter to which my hon. friend has referred, I may say that the report of rumoured abuses in the army postal service in Vancouver came to my attention early this week. While I was not given any actual evidence of the truth of these rumours, I nevertheless immediately ordered an investigation, which is at present in progress. So far nothing has come to light to indicate that there is any truth in these rumours.
As hon. members well know, postal investigations are most effectively carried through when the parties involved are unaware of the inquiry, and I can only hope that the effectiveness of this particular inquiry will not be prejudiced by what appears to be a particularly highly coloured and as yet unsubstantiated newspaper story.
With regard to the hon. member's second question, I understand that if a soldier has served abroad less than a year he may bring back $100 worth of goods free of duty. If he has served for a year or longer there is no limit on the amount he can bring back, but it must have been purchased at least six months prior to his returning to Canada. This applies no matter where the service abroad has been, whether in the United States, the Far East or Germany. I think it is covered by items 703(b) and (c) of the tariff act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ASSINIBOINE RIVER-INQUIRY AS TO RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIKES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the items that we are dealing with under this heading relate to the most challenging prospect that Canadians have before them today. While all of the area known as the north may not be under the administration of the minister of this department, we must always be conscious of the fact that well over two-thirds of the land mass of Canada is in an area that we may freely describe as "the north". The phrase "the north" is a variable term. For a long time North Bay has been regarded as the gateway to the north in Ontario; and yet North Bay is far south of Edmonton, is only about the same distance north as the city of Quebec, and by the standards of those who live in the prairie provinces could hardly be regarded as a northern city by any accurate description. While it may not be easy to define the actual area that we would describe as the north, I believe that we may generally regard it as the area above the substantially settled communities across Canada. The north stretches from Labrador across to the Yukon and embraces all that great territory up to the Arctic ocean.
There has been evidence that the minister has shown considerable interest in the activities of his department, but certainly I was not only disturbed, but amazed to hear the attitude of the minister summed up in the words that there must be jobs in the north before the people will go there. It is that statement, and the fact that the minister apparently continues to accept that as a definition of his opinion, that impel me to make these remarks which I now propose to make while we are in committee, in regard to the affairs of this department.
The north in Canada now represents the great challenging area of development. It seems to me that the approach to the development of the north must be the same kind of approach as that which inspired our forefathers to extend railway lines across Canada, and build canals at a time when there was apparently no shipping to justify that immense expenditure for those days. Think of the imagination and the faith in the future that was represented by those who constructed the Canadian Pacific Railway. Think of the courage and the willingness to pledge the credit of Canada for the future of Canada that was represented by the decision of the government of Sir John Macdonald in 1881 to make the necessary arrangements with the company which was to build that great line across this country. Just let us recall-and particularly let our youth today recall-the vision of the men and women of those days.
The western territories were largely populated by roaming Indian tribes and by great
[The Deputy Chairman.]

herds of buffalo. As the Canadian Pacific lines were driven west, the builders were confronted with attacks by Indian tribes, and they were also, I might say, confronted by very severe attacks from some of the people who did not like to see their land used for that purpose, people who expressed their feelings with some vigour. But this line was driven across Canada, not because there were jobs there but because it was felt that with the resources across that great territory this railway development would create the possibility of jobs. Then it was left up to the initiative, courage and vigour of men and women with adventurous spirit to go out and make the jobs in the area, that vast area where transportation had been made available in that way.
Let us come to a later period, the thirties, when the expansion of northwestern Canada was taking place. Surely one of the most romantic chapters of Canadian history is the opening of the mineral and fur-bearing areas of northwestern Canada by air transport. It happens that I had the privilege, first, of visiting many of those far northern areas as a youngster. But later, some 20 years ago, I flew through most of that great territory from the Atlantic to the Pacific in those single-engined machines which were at that time carrying the largest freight load carried by any country in the world-surely something of which Canadians have reason to be proud today. It stirs the blood when you look back at those bush pilots who were carrying in those comparatively light Fairchilds, Fokkers and Junkers this immense load, greater in total than the total air freight load of the United States or of any other country in the world. That opened up the mining areas of Slave lake and Great Bear lake. It opened up the territories along the Mackenzie river, over to the Yukon, across to Hudson bay, and on, eastward, right over through the whole of northern Quebec and Labrador. What a challenging picture to the youth of today! Those men did not have jobs waiting for them there; they made the jobs. They reached out to the new territories and they created the possibilities of jobs with the transportation they themselves were supplying. It seems to me that this is the spirit in which we must approach this immense opportunity, this almost unlimited opportunity, which has opened out before us across this whole northland of ours. We are not speaking about some vague and uncertain thing. Across that whole area are resources such as are hardly equalled either elsewhere in Canada or elsewhere in the world. Sometimes I find that people who actually were not born and brought up here seem to see some of these things more clearly than we ourselves do.

I recall that it is more than 25 years ago- yes, nearly 30 years ago-when in a speech in Toronto the Right Hon. L. M. S. Amery made a statement which at that time seemed to me to be almost beyond the realm of reality, namely that in the great Pre-Cambrian shield and the northland generally of Canada there was mineral wealth yet to be discovered beyond anything discovered in any other country in the world today.
The time came when I saw some of that reality. I remember flying into the uranium discovery at Great Bear lake in the early stages, just after it had been opened up. That discovery had much to do with the ending of the Japanese war and, perhaps some of us might say, with all the terrible consequences that have flowed from the discovery made possible by the use of Canadian uranium at that time. But also in that area, as is known by everyone who has been there, there are fantastic deposits of silver, copper and other metals waiting to be developed. Yes, and throughout the whole north, there is iron in quantities equalled nowhere else in the world today. There is oil as well and gas in that far northland, as distinguished from the gas and oil of the southern areas. There is coal and above all there is waterpower. Every one of the great sources of industrial energy is there in that vast northland starting with the huge falls on the Hamilton river on the east coast of Labrador, right across to the mighty waterways of the Yukon and of the Northwest Territories. The possibilities for development are simply staggering. One of the rather remarkable affinities of nature is the fact that almost invariably the minerals are found in proximity to waterpower which can be turned into electric energy. There is lead and there is zinc as well in those areas.
To show that this is by no manner of means some vague and uncertain thing, may I say that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company have 1,200 claims in the Pine Point area and are actually going ahead with underground work as soon as it is practical. Throughout the whole of that broad northland the challenge is there to all Canadians and to the young people from other parts of the world as well as to the people not so young but who are young in spirit. I know my hon. friend will share that view because he is indeed young in spirit himself.
One could go on to deal with these great opportunities. I have not mentioned nickel or some of the other metals that are found in such great quantities there. On the Mackenzie river, near Fort Good Hope there is a vast power potential. On the south Nahanni river there is Virginia falls, a waterfall twice as large as Niagara. On the Lockhart river
Supply-Northern Affairs at the east end of Great Slave lake there are enormous power resources. At Dead Man's rapids on the Slave river near Fort Smith there is a drop of 110 feet in ten miles, with a huge power potential. Power is also being developed in great quantities at Yellowknife for the operation of the mines there.
This is not without its accompanying resources as well because there are agricultural resources in those areas. Actually, the Mackenzie river plain is an extension of the prairie land of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Also there is wood in marketable quantities throughout that area. Along the Slave river, the Mackenzie river and the Liard river areas there are wonderful possibilities for agriculture. Things grow there rapidly in the long days of sunlight. Those who have been through that area also recognize the fact that, apart from the magnificent growth of food and vegetables, nowhere else in Canada are there flowers of such great brilliance and increasing in brilliance right up to the Arctic, from Aklavik right across to Coppermine, which is to the northeast, and to Hudson bay.
All this calls for unlimited optimism. All this calls for basing our plans upon the practical foundation of demonstrated hope that these things can become a reality in the years ahead. If we had waited until we saw the jobs or, shall I say, if our forefathers had waited until the jobs were there, the prairies would not have developed nor would the areas farther north to which branch lines from the Canadian Pacific railway have been extended. In Ontario, if the Ontario Northland Railway in the earlier part of this century had not been built up to James bay through an area which was still wild and where there was no real development at all at that time, the rich part of northern Ontario perhaps would still be in a primitive state today. But transportation was provided which made it possible for men and women of spirit and initiative to go there and to make jobs.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that this is not something to be left to reckless or haphazard development. We all know that mineral resources are wasting resources. We know that if there is inferior or inadequate transportation, only the richest ores will be highgraded and that promising mines will be left in a condition that may hardly make it economic for years to come to resume development. It is therefore important that under a free economy-and certainly under no shackles of socialism-we provide sensible plans, recognizing these vast potentialities, which will integrate the development with

Supply-Northern Affairs the resources and will provide the transportation into the areas where, by one means or another, these vast power potentials are going to be developed.
Without embarking on any acrimonious reference to an earlier discussion about what was known as the public investment program may I suggest that, to the extent that the government still feels that the credit of Canada should be pledged to a national development program, there is no place where this can better be done than throughout that northland where millions of horsepower of electric energy are waiting to be harnessed for the advantage of new generations if we place the credit of Canada behind that development.
I have heard it said that we must not be reckless in expenditures. As a Conservative, I trust that we shall be conservative in our approach to the handling of our finances in this respect. But, Mr. Chairman, there is a difference between spending money on capital development and spending money, on which there is no return, on some passing phase of our activities. This is capital development of the most valuable kind from which the returns will be not tenfold but one hundredfold in the years ahead in the communities that will grow there in that great northern area. That is a place in which to try out plans for development.
Then, Mr. Chairman, there is another aspect to this matter that I think we have perhaps overlooked, namely national defence. We have two-thirds of the land mass of our country with a sparse and limited population. It is of vital importance to the defence of Canada that communities be established near these power resources under an integrated plan right through the whole of northern Canada. Let no young person shudder with the thought of cold and worry about the prospect of going into the northland. About ten days ago a number of members of the house visited the military establishment at Churchill. Every one of them came back enthusiastic about the conditions under which the people were living at Churchill. I am confident that the minister, in giving the population of the northern areas, has not included the military establishments.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ASSINIBOINE RIVER-INQUIRY AS TO RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIKES
speechtext: Churchill is below the 60th parallel. It is in Manitoba.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ASSINIBOINE RIVER-INQUIRY AS TO RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIKES
speechtext: I realize that, and I indicated that I realized that. Quite apart from the arbitrary definition, I am talking about the great northland and not only the Northwest Territories.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ASSINIBOINE RIVER-INQUIRY AS TO RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIKES
speechtext: I am not quarrelling with you about it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ASSINIBOINE RIVER-INQUIRY AS TO RESPONSIBILITY FOR DIKES
speechtext:
I realize that the area under the immediate administration of the department and the Northwest Territories council, whose jurisdiction has been greatly expanded within the period that the minister has been the head of the department, starts at the 60th parallel. In the same way that North Bay is not really north, as I pointed out, there is also a lot of land south of the 60th parallel that most of us would regard as very far north indeed, and most of us definitely regard Churchill, halfway up the coast of Hudson bay, as very far north by ordinary standards. That was what I meant when I said that the word "north" is a broad, embracing term which includes within it the defined areas beginning at the 60th parallel. What I really wanted to point out with regard to Churchill was that in an area that is cold by any standards and in fact, I understand, is inclined to be a little colder than even the Arctic coast, those who live there find it healthy and invigorating, and I have had reports from young men there who believe they are in the very best military establishment in the whole of Canada. It is always a good thing for people, wherever they are, to believe they are in the best military establishment.
I mention that because it is only indicative of what is happening. Right across the whole northern part of Canada, without going into details that should not be placed on the record, there are air bases and radar bases which today embrace a substantial population. There is already a population there living perhaps not with all the amenities of the deep south of Canada but nevertheless living a vigorous, healthy and, to them, an invigorating and rewarding life. I mention that because if military bases can be agreeable places to live in, then civilian bases organized on a similar plan, such as would surround great hydroelectric developments producing 500,000, 1 million horsepower, and so on, would be similarly attractive places for people to live. After all, there were many people who found the Yukon and Dawson City a very pleasant place in the early days and not entirely as primitive as described by Robert W. Service in his wonderful poems. There are many members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and of other Canadian services who have found service life pleasant throughout the northland. But it would be very wise for us to make sure that with the development of these natural resources we have communities spotted across the north, because the real threat to Canada might come from parachute troops dropped over that northern area. Airports

should be developed all across the area farther south of the northern air and radar bases where appropriate steps could be taken to deal with a situation of that kind.
This is a reality if the danger of war is a reality at all. If we are spending over $2 billion with the recognition of the real danger of the possibility of war, then we must recognize the existence of the possibility of war and we must remember that the closest nation to Canada with the exception of the United States is Russia. We must remember that Russia is separated from the North American continent only by the Bering strait, 55 miles wide, and that northeastern China along the Yalu river is not many hours flying time from northern Canada in modern transport machines. While all of us hope and pray that war may not come, we cannot disregard the promise made yesterday by Chou En-lai that in the event of war China would stand side by side with Russia. We therefore see on the other side of the Pacific over 700 million people from whom units can be drawn that might be moved by air into that area.
This is a part of the problem of national defence. I mention it because it was said: You are not going to spend money on a large scale in the north. Money spent there should be regarded first of all as long-term self-liquidating returnable capital and, second, it should be regarded in the light of its value to national defence. I do not intend to enlarge upon these remarks beyond repeating my conviction as one who has seen that area grow from the most primitive stage, when on the north coast there were only Eskimos, the R.C.M.P. and the wireless stations, to the point where it has become integrated fairly well into our society through air development.
Let us look ahead. I would not suggest railway facilities, but there are roads. There is also the fantastic development in air transport. Last September at Farnborough I saw one of the new Blackburn transports take on board and carry away a huge truck. I saw two complete 25-pounder units with ammunition wagons go into one of these Blackburn transports, and saw them flown away. I mention that because we have reached the point now where nearly anything that can be moved by rail can be moved by the huge air transports now being produced. This development has revolutionized the whole prospects of the north. We should have no limit to our optimism and our hopes for that area. I trust that the plans of the government will be consonant with the spirit of the people of Canada and that when we say "go north, young man,
Supply-Northern Affairs go north" we will not tell him there is going to be a comfortable job ready and waiting for him but that we will take steps that will assure that his vigour, initiative and courage can be rewarded by opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the Leader of the Opposition. He has made the kind of speech I should like to make and have made on occasion about the development of the north, a challenge and necessity in our day. The Leader of the Opposition has made a comparison that has been made in the past, and which I have used, between the west of 50 years and more ago and the north today. It is true that when the Canadian Pacific Railway was built through the west it meant for the people of that day the meeting of a great challenge. It was constructed at a time when there was a population of about 4 million in Canada and the national income was very low compared with what it is today. Our forefathers, even our fathers, certainly took risks at the time, met the challenge, and the west was opened because transportation was furnished.
I said yesterday that the key to the economic development and opening up of the north is cheaper transportation. That is what brought about the development of the west. But there is a difference between the opening up of the west and the opening up of the north in this sense, that our forefathers, our grandfathers, could go to the west with this new means of transportation, open up the country and settle on farms with no more than their bare hands. This is not the kind of development that we can expect north of the 60th parallel. It will be mainly mineral development. Mineral development requires capital investment in huge quantities. It requires also, and I repeat it, cheaper transportation.
As I said yesterday, we should first create an economic climate that will be attractive to capital. In order to help do that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is conducting intensive geological surveys. We are studying now the possibility of improving transportation facilities in the north and of making it cheaper. We believe that we have to provide cheaper transportation, as was done in the west, in order that the north may be developed and populated. The populating of the north is not a primary aim in itself; it is, in point of time, secondary. Really, it comes after the necessary provision for the development of the immense natural resources to which the Leader of the Opposition so eloquently referred.
Well, making provision for that development is what we are doing, and I pray to

Supply-Northern Affairs God that this generation will have the same spirit of adventure, the same pioneering spirit that our fathers and forefathers had. With that spirit we can develop these northern parts that have to be developed. The day is near when the resources of northern Canada will be badly needed in the world, especially the mineral resources. But so far as transportation is concerned, although I have great confidence in aviation I cannot foresee the day-although it may come sooner than I think-when the huge air transports to which the Leader of the Opposition was referring could be used economically for the transportation of mineral concentrates from the north to the smelters. Of course, one could say that we should build smelters up there; that we have the power. It is true that we have the power but these are very costly operations.
For instance, in the case of the Pine Point discoveries on the south shore of Great Slave lake, there lies there what we believe to be the greatest known ore body of lead and zinc. We hope that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company will soon see fit to have definite plans for the development and exploitation of this vast ore body. We hope that it will be possible to work out with them some kind of arrangement under which transportation facilities will be available to take out the ore. I have said, both outside the house and in the committee, that we hope it will be possible in days not too far off to have what is still the cheapest kind of transportation for distances of 300 or 400 miles or more, and that is a railway line from Grimshaw to Pine Point. We have been discussing, and still are discussing, the economic implications of such a project.
We look at the north, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition has said, and I thank him for his intervention, as something that has to be developed, not in a haphazard way but with plans. The plans must be directed not so much towards putting people there for the sake of putting people there, but towards exploiting the resources. We should first have capital which will go there because the economic climate will have been created by cheaper transportation. Then, these natural resources will be developed and manpower will go there because the capital investment which is necessary will have been made. Then, the population will go there, and I am sure that the population will be happy because in Whitehorse, Yellowknife and even far north in Aklavik I have met and talked to people who were very happy with their lot in life. The north presents a great challenge to all Canadians, and I hope that all hon.

members in this house will help the government, will help me and the officials of my department, to meet that challenge in the national interests.

Mr. Chairman, we have just heard two interesting speeches, to which I, for one, have listened most attentively. I wish to congratulate my leader, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), as well as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) on their eloquent pleas on behalf of northern Canada.
Mr. Chairman, the Quebec battlefields commission, about which I would like to offer a few remarks, comes under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
Last year, while we were discussing these estimates, the minister asked the house to increase from $100,000 to $125,000 the annual amount which the commission uses in its operations. The house unanimously agreed to this request from the minister.
This year, according to the estimates, the same amount seems to be required. A year ago I appealed to the minister to see to it, if it were at all possible, that this $25,000 increase be used to increase the salaries of the employees of this commission, who, as far as I can see, do not receive what they possibly could earn elsewhere, in trade or industry. The minister told me he would pay particular attention to this request. Now, I would not like to be accused of narrowmindedness, and I do wish to render unto Caesar what is Caesar's, but following that, I received other requests. It was pointed out to me among other things that one employee in particular, who had been working for the commission for 16 years, was only being paid 99 cents an hour, whereas others doing the same work were earning considerably more. I took up the matter with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. It was he who spoke for me, and indirectly, for the employee in question. I am happy to tell the house that in this one case which I took up with the minister, we received full and complete satisfaction. I do want to thank the minister for doing what he had resolved to do, and I hope that other such increases may be granted during the 1955-56 fiscal year.
I am sure the minister will agree with me when I say that certain employees, whether employed on a temporary basis, for the summer season only, or on a permanent basis, are not getting salaries consistent with the

work they perform. Here again I trust that the minister's sense of fair play will induce him to get for these employees the salary they deserve.
I understand, Mr. Chairman, that the Quebec national battlefields are to undergo a certain restoration again this year. These battlefields are an historical site unequalled,
I think, in North America, if not in the world. We have there a page of history which our people like to relive now and then and which other people want to see.
The Quebec national battlefields represent also a substantial source of revenue for our city. As a matter of fact, these battlefields alone constitute an industry, a tourist industry, if you like, but which is bringing us visitors from everywhere. In Quebec City, we often say, referring to tourist advertising, that they come to our city in order to see what is not to be seen anywhere else. This is very true. City people are not interested in visiting big cities. They are looking for something new, and that is what we have to offer; the Quebec national battlefields are most interesting for those who are visiting the city of Quebec.
All tourists from overseas land in Wolfe's cove-a magnificent harbour built by a Conservative government at the request of one of my distinguished predecessors, the Hon. Maurice Dupre-and head straight for the battlefields.
The hon. minister was so kind as to tell me the other day that repair work will be done on Gilmour Hill road, which leads to the battlefields, and has regrettably suffered during our hard winter.
I trust, Mr. Chairman, that the funds we are going to vote for this commission will be reasonably spent and, again, I hope that the hon. Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will speak to the members of the commission on behalf of the workers who are paid low salaries and obtain for them decent wages, which will enable them to face their family obligations.
Mr. Chairman, a moment ago, the Leader of the Opposition, the head of the party to which I belong, made a most interesting statement about our northern regions and more particularly about the region where one of the most important of our military camps is established, i.e., Fort Churchill. I had the privilege recently of visiting that northern establishment as well as several settlements
Supply-Northern Affairs in Manitoba. I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to thank the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) for the chance he gave many members of the house to visit that part of our Canadian north. I would be remiss if I did not also thank the member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) who at all times did all he could to make that trip a memorable one.
Apart from the military, we met, in The Pas area, various people engaged in public life. The mayor of The Pas, the president of the board of trade, people belonging to various social organizations asked us to support their representative in the House of Commons in his requests to the government that the northern regions be given particular consideration since they hold untold riches which constitute a source of immense wealth for the entire country. Mr. Chairman, the members of this group have always been particularly interested in the conservation and development of our natural resources and on that account we are very interested in the estimates of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. I have read with great care the minutes of the proceedings of the committee on estimates for the period when it was dealing with the minister's department, and I found there a lot of valuable information. I do not intend to take up the time of the committee in asking questions which were answered as a result of the discussions in the committee.
The visit which the minister made to British Columbia was greatly appreciated by the persons he met. It indicated an interest on the part of the minister and a desire to see things at first hand and discuss them with his officials on the spot. I think that is to be commended. I have been asked by a number of organizations in Kootenay West to extend an invitation to the minister to visit our district and endeavour to address at least a few meetings. There are many problems in my constituency about which the people are greatly interested. I hope he will find time during the coming recess of parliament to visit the constituency and see the many things we have to show and listen to what my constituents will have to tell him. I am sure that as a result of contact with my constituents he will have even a greater understanding of the problems they face and the difficulties they encounter.


In my opinion the minister through his department holds the key to the promotion and conservation and development of our natural resources. He is in a strategic position in my opinion to give a lead by this understanding of these problems and the necessity for the proper development of our resources, finally resulting in a national policy of soil, water and forest conservation.
The minister's activities to date have clearly indicated his interest in the conservation of our natural resources and their proper development, particularly the water resources of the Columbia. I have had a number of letters from constituents who had noted with interest the minister's attention to that problem which is so important to many people in Kootenay West.
Under this first item I want to make a few suggestions to the minister which I believe *come within the ambit of administration. I do not intend to speak at length. In my opinion a satisfactory development of a conservation policy in this country demands public understanding, public appreciation, public interest and public support. I think in this field of government activity knowledge on the part of the public is essential. It has come to my attention from time to time that many Canadians are unaware of the work being done by the various branches of the minister's department and the relationship of that work to the development of our natural resources and their conservation.
I suppose it would be correct to say that the national parks branch of the minister's department is the best known. A great number of Canadians know about our national parks, but even that best known branch is not known to many Canadians.
The engineering and water resources branch is doing a work of immense value but few Canadians realize the value of this work and the extent of the investigations being carried on on the Columbia and other river systems and in other places in Canada. Large-scale investigations have been going on in my constituency for some ten years but still there are many people who are uninformed as to this work and its value and place in the final development of the water resources of our area.
I have had this matter in mind for some time because I see the great need for doing something along the lines that I am about to suggest. In my opinion there is a necessity, particularly in the minister's department, for

greater public relations activity so that the public may be fully informed of the work of the department and its various branches. I suggest that this could be done by means of frequent press releases to the newspapers and national magazines and through other publicity media.
It could be done also by the minister and his senior officials making occasional addresses. I would not suggest that the Minister of Finance would get a hearty welcome if he were to go around addressing farmers on taxation, as that is not a popular subject. But this is one case where I think there is an opportunity for the minister to address public bodies, because the work of this department is quite popular and I am sure people would appreciate hearing from the minister and his officials.
The northern affairs branch has greatly increased its activities in recent years. I listened with interest to the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition. There is a growing interest in the development of the northern parts of Canada. I do not think it is quite fair to suggest that there has been little done in the development of the north. I have been perusing the estimates for the last five or six years and, if my calculations are correct, since the hon. member for the Yukon came to this house-I see him in his seat- expenditures in the Yukon have increased about fifteenfold.

Here again there is a great lack of understanding and knowledge with respect to northern affairs by the great majority of Canadians. I suggest that this is another opportunity for the public relations branch of the minister's department to do something to inform Canadians to a greater extent about this important part of his administration.
I have been a lumberjack for a good many years. I made my living from a combination of farming and logging. Therefore I am particularly interested in the work of the
Supply-Northern Affairs forestry branch of the minister's department. The behind-the-scenes work of the men in the forestry branch of the minister's department goes almost unrecognized by the majority of Canadians, and I have always rather resented that. It is recognized by those who are particularly concerned with what they are doing or particularly wish to follow it; that is, some of the people in the universities, some of those in the larger lumber companies, and a few other people who are particularly interested in the development of conservation policies and matters of that sort. But the work of that branch goes largely unrecognized by the majority of Canadians. The research work conducted by the forest products laboratories in Vancouver and Ottawa and the other activities of the branch are almost unknown to the Canadian people generally.
I suggest again, Mr. Chairman, that this excellent scientific work and investigation and its results should be publicized to a greater extent through the press, through national magazines and through any other media that the minister saw fit. I suggest that, if we are going to obtain an understanding of the development of our natural resources and an appreciation of what they mean to Canada at the present time and in the days to come, we have to disseminate more information. We have to get the cooperation of a much wider group of Canadians. I suggest that the minister would be well advised to keep agricultural organizations, labour organizations, women's institutes and women's national organizations informed, and also to keep all the universities informed and find some means of bringing this information to the attention of the schools across Canada. I have great faith in getting this sort of concrete, definite information regarding government policies and actions with respect to natural resources brought to the attention of the children. I believe that the question of the conservation and development of natural resources should be brought to their attention beginning just after the primary grades in the public schools of this country.
An informed public opinion will develop increasing support for larger expenditures on policies designed to conserve our natural resources. Therefore I suggest that the minister will be well advised to explore all suitable avenues through which he can properly inform the public of the important work of his department and what that work means to this country. There is no real protection for our natural resources except that protection which is based on the strength of an informed

Supply-Northern Affairs public opinion and an aroused public conscience. In that connection, I should like to bring to the minister's attention and to the attention of members of this house a most interesting article which I recently read in the May 14 issue of Saturday Night. This article was written by Mr. Roderick Haig-Brown, who has been a great advocate of conservation policies in British Columbia for many years. The minister may know this gentleman. He has been a great defender of our provincial parks, our forest resources and our natural resources against the continuing intrusion of industrialism into our province. This article is entitled "The Vanishing Park-lands and Public Conscience". I am going to read only the concluding paragraph of the article, because I thought he put in excellent language and in brief form a sentiment that should be supported by all members in this house. This is what Mr. Roderick Haig-Brown has to say in concluding this article:
But there is, ultimately, no real protection for parks except in the strength of public feeling. So long as the public turns and bows three times in the direction of the nearest stock exchange at every mention of "progress" or "industrial development", provincial legislatures can be depended upon to make mad decisions about parks,-
I should like to bring to the attention of the house, and I am very happy to say this, that the public of Kootenay West did not bow three times in front of the stock exchange at the mention of a prospective industrial development. Then he goes on to say:
-and even the federal government will bear watching. There will be hope of a comprehensive and secure parks system in Canada the first time a labour union votes to down tools because a project threatens a park, or the first time an aroused citizenry mans a picket line in defence of a park. Sooner or later both these things will happen. But in the meantime the parks are disappearing.
He is referring to our provincial parks in British Columbia. Those remarks can apply equally well to the conservation of our natural resources in general. Therefore, because of my belief that knowledge is essential for widespread public support in defence of our natural resources, I bring these suggestions to the minister and trust he will find some ways and means of informing to a much greater extent the public of this country and the school children of this country of the value of the work of his department as a part of a national conservation policy in Canada.

I like often to recall-and my leader this afternoon has reminded us of it-the days of the building of the C.P.R., because it was, after all, a business epic; it was a business romance. I suggest that anyone who has not read it should look up a narrative poem by Professor Pratt, I believe, of Victoria University, called "Toward the Last Spike". There he will find courage of the highest type in two quarters. First of all among the builders of the road. I like to think of Sir William Van Horne, an office man who could walk across a chasm on a plank where the workmen would only go on their hands and knees. That is the kind of man he was. I like to think also of this house when, in answer to many doubting hearts, Sir Charles Tupper, who was being jeered at-those were the days when it was said the railroad would never pay for the axle grease-made the heroic answer, "I can bear the jeers of hon. gentlemen opposite; I await the plaudits of posterity". I should like to make a slight reference to one aspect of this matter. I believe we have this on a better basis this afternoon than last night. I quite realize that the minister has other people to whom he has to pay some deference, such as a hardhearted Minister of Finance and so on. Recent remarks by the hon. member for Bow River have prompted me to participate briefly in this debate. As you will recall, the hon. member was at some pains to set the record straight. I thought perhaps I might follow his good example for a few moments. The hon. member went into considerable detail as to the glories of Banff national park. While I would not argue with him seriously in regard to his claim that it is an outstanding tourist attraction, nevertheless I would remind him that there is a park somewhat to the north of that, known as Jasper national park, which has within its borders, or close to them, the highest peak in the Canadian Rockies. I am referring to mount Robson. Considerable publicity comes to the Jasper park region because of the fact that we have there, as I say, the highest peak in the Canadian Rockies.
Coming to this matter of putting the record straight, Mr. Chairman, I felt that I should like to remind hon. members who come from these flat lands of the east that after all they should not allow the Canadian Rockies to so overawe them that they overlook the fact that in reality the Canadian Rockies are merely the foothills of our mighty Coast range of mountains in British Columbia. Some indication that this is the prevailing attitude in the east is found in an article that I recall noticing about a year ago in the Toronto Star Weekly, which went to considerable pains to describe mount Robson, referring to it as the highest mountain in Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether you observed that article, but I am quite sure you will agree with me that that was not a correct statement of fact, and that it is something which perhaps could be put straight in the minds of those who dwell in the more easterly parts of Canada.
As you are undoubtedly well aware, within the present boundaries of the constituency of Comox-Alberni, in a part of our country which, I believe, at one time was within the constituency which you represent, Mr. Chairman, does lie the highest mountain in Canada, namely mighty mount Waddington, at the head of Knight inlet in the Klinaklini river area, the only mountain as far as I know which rises above 13,000 feet.

I felt that I should like to put the record straight, and in view of the discussion that has taken place about the biggest and best national parks in Canada, draw to the attention of the minister that when he is looking around for bigger and better national parks in Canada, there in the western part of British Columbia does in fact lie Canada's mightiest mountain, rising to something over 13,200 feet.

Mr. Chairman, whilst some hon. members may have been a little jealous about the attractions of Banff as a national park, there is really no doubt in anybody's mind that Banff is the greatest tourist attraction in Canada today. However, many of the people who come to Banff are very much disappointed at the very poor fishing they find. They read the "Anglers' Guide" and are told that some of the lakes and streams are teeming with fish. Then after having fished there for a week and having caught one fish, or none at all, they begin to wonder where these teeming lakes are.
I was very much interested in an article that appeared in the "Voice of Motordom" the official organ of the A.M.A., by Fred Turnbull, president of the Edmonton trout fishing club. I should like to quote briefly from that article. He was first of all referring to the great improvement in fishing in the province of Alberta as a result of the recent conservation program. Then he had this to say:
What has been the effect of this great local improvement on the tourist influx to our national parks? We all like to go to the mountains to fish and at the same time enjoy the wonderful scenery, but place before the fisherman two choices, one, to visit the national park and to enjoy the scenery but along with that obtain only mediocre fishing, and on the other hand drive out 30 miles or so from the city after lunch and return home with an excellent catch of trout up to four pounds in weight. It is left to the reader to say which choice the fisherman will take.
There is no doubt that those responsible for the very mediocre fishing in our national parks are beginning to realize that the tourist expects something more than pictures of used fish displayed in travel and sporting magazines with the caption "Come to Canada and get the big ones". What does the average tourist fisherman expect? It is generally conceded that the average fisherman is satisfied with a reasonable catch of say four or five trout about a half a pound to two pounds each with the occasional big one as an added incentive. He wants these fish in lakes and streams fairly close to the highway, not so far away that he has to hire an expensive outfit to reach them.
I have heard many reasons for the poor fishing in the national parks in the Rockies.

Let us not penalize the people who want the right to haul where they wish. I say that argument does not hold water. I think possibly there are a great many people who question the proposition of being able to haul their grain here or there, where there is a difference. The other day in this house an hon. member said he would not want to bind himself unconditionally to any one line elevator company at the present time.
I just cannot see any point in that argument. As far as I am concerned every line elevator in western Canada is exactly the same. You will get just as good a deal from the line elevator companies, as far as grade, dockage and weight are concerned, as you will from the pool elevators. They are good. They have to be good because of the fact that the pool elevators are handling a great quantity of the farmers' grain. That has not always been the history of the line elevator companies, and therein lies the crux of the whole situation.
Too many of us remember what happened before the pool elevator system started to handle a great deal of the farmers' grain. You would go to the line elevator, and you had to take No. 4 grade for No. 2 wheat. It was a case of take it or leave it. You were overdocked, underweighed and undergraded. These were the conditions that made the farmers decide to shift for themselves and form the pool elevator system, in order to get away from the discrimination that- was being practised.
I say that is the crux of the whole situation. With the formation of the pool elevator 50433-237
Canada Grain Act
system of grain handling those practices came to an end. You will get just as good a deal now from the line elevator companies as you will from the pools. You will continue to get that kind of deal just as long as the pool elevators are in business. But just as soon, as the pools go out of business you are going to get the same kind of deal you got before they came into existence.
The line companies are trying to woo customers from the pools by promises of a better deal. Their efforts in this direction are being aided by the government, when pool members are not afforded the opportunity of delivering grain to their own elevators, which they themselves built in order that they might participate in the savings made through handling their own grain, amounting to millions of dollars annually. That is what we object to. It is often said that one picture is worth a thousand words. Sometimes a story is equally useful for the purpose of emphasizing a point. I am not going to say any more on the subject, but I should like to tell a little story to emphasize the point I am trying to make.
The present efforts of the line companies, abetted by the government, to restore their monopoly position so far as the grain trade is concerned, are reminiscent of a story I heard many years ago about an old farmer who had nieces and nephews. They placed a herd of cattle in the old farmer's care in trust, and he was to look after the cattle for them. Bands of marauding wolves throughout the countryside were taking a heavy toll of the herd so the old farmer, true to his trust, built a stout corral and hired range riders who guarded the herd by day. Oh, once in a while a wily wolf crashed the corral at night and grabbed a calf, but the system worked pretty well. All the wolves could do was stay out in the hills, hold indignation meetings and wonder what they could do about it.

The nieces and nephews, like a great many people, fell prey to propaganda. As a result they went to the old farmer and said they thought they should be getting a greater return from the herd. Under pressure the old farmer hired another manager, with specific instructions to cut down on the costs. The operation had to be made more efficient. The new manager thought about the matter for a long time and came up with an idea. He reasoned that wolves, because of their long experience and wide knowledge, knew more about cattle than anybody else. So he summoned the wolves to a big conference, and they really co-operated. Hearings were held

Canada Grain Act
and committees appointed, all at the expense of the old farmer, of course.
Finally all the wolves were unanimous in their opinion. They said tear down the corral, it is unproductive; fire all the range riders, they are nothing but arbitrary bureaucrats. When all the reports had been made the old farmer questioned the new manager as to whether or not this was the right thing to do. The manager said it must be right, because the committees he had set up knew more about cattle than anybody else.
It is the same with those who speak against the measure before us today. Why should they not accede to the wishes and advice of the line elevator companies? After all, they have had 50 years' experience, and they certainly know more about the grain business than the farmers themselves.
Regardless of the outcome of the vote, which may be taken today, we are going to continue to fight for this fundamental principle, so that the farmers may be able to deliver their grain to elevators of their own choosing.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill represents the third attempt by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) to have legislation of this type enacted. As Bill No. 186 it was introduced into the previous parliament on February 23, 1953. Subsequently as Bill No. 3 it was introduced on November 16, 1953, at the first session of this parliament. It was defeated on January 15, 1954, by 111 votes to 29.
The hon. member persists in spite of the adverse opinion which this house has already recorded on his proposal. He persists in spite of the fact that his plan is completely unworkable, as he could have ascertained by application to any company operating elevators in western Canada. He persists in spite of the fact that during sessions of the agriculture committee last May there was extensive discussion about car allocation, during which the hon. member and his colleagues were unable to elicit one word of approval from witnesses who apeared before that body.
The house will wish not to be wearied by unnecessary repetition of what was said in the debate last year. For example, at page 937 of Hansard for December 15, 1953, an extensive statement was placed on record in connection with the car order book and its history. That need not be repeated. But it must be repeated that the car order book already provides all that is necessary to enable a grain producer to have placed at the elevator of his choice a car for the loading of his own grain.
tMr. Bryson.]
The car order book provisions are an invaluable safeguard of a farmer's rights, whether he chooses to order cars, as he sometimes does, or refrains from doing so. The latter is the case at most times, in most places with most farmers. The effect of this bill would be to force the car order book into constant use at those points where farmers now elect not to use it. It would provide a certain arbitrary distribution of box cars at such a point, a distribution which, presumably advantageous to one elevator or another, might be objectionable to some other elevator or to some producer. The operation of such a scheme would at once be brought to naught by the first person, whether elevator agent or farmer, who chose to put his name on the car order book. That is one reason why the scheme is unworkable.
Observe next that the proposed legislation would be completely unenforceable. It seeks to place a duty upon the railway agent, at any given moment, to act in a prescribed way. But who would ascertain his duty at such a moment? Who could say whether or not he had acted correctly? Who could say that he was not planning to remedy any apparent defect in his procedure at some date, sooner or later, in the future? Or think of the task of the railway agent at one of the larger shipping points where there may be from 300 to 1,300 permit books, covering perhaps 100,000 seeded acres or more, and where there are perhaps seven or eight elevators. At Dawson Creek over 1,300 permit books are issued annually, with an acreage of 260,000. He would have a highly involved arithmetical calculation to make before he could arrive at a basis for car distribution. There would be room for a multiplicity of errors, with perhaps no answer possible that would be both acceptable and practicable. And to add to his confusion would be the knowledge that error would put him in peril of the penalties prescribed for violations of the Canada Grain Act.
The bill provides for a sort of election, with votes weighted according to acreage. Such a scheme is loaded with difficulties. An acre which has been intended to produce fodder in the shape of green feed will have equal voting rights with one which has actually produced 30 bushels of wheat. An acre on which the crop has been destroyed by hail, by rust or by frost will have equal rights with a nearby acre which has had a good crop. An acre producing five bushels of flax will have equal rights with an acre which has produced 100 bushels of oats.
Observe next that the farmer who is willing to take the trouble can vote twice, to the

disadvantage of his neighbour who does not want to be put to this trouble. He can first vote his full acreage in favour of one elevator. Then, having done so, he can put his name on the car order book for successive cars to accommodate all the marketable grain he has produced, for shipment from that elevator. Or, having voted his acreage in favour of one elevator, he may actually deliver to another.
The hon. member last year seemed willing to admit that there were in his bill certain weaknesses, as had been pointed out. He went on to say on January 15, 1954, Hansard, at page 1169:
I submit that is no reason for defeating this bill. Rather the subject matter of the bill should be referred to the agriculture committee of this house for discussion and consideration.
But the difficulties and defects to be found in the bill are not simple matters of wording or of drafting which can be ironed out by revision. Instead, defects are inherent in the very concept of the scheme. Moreover, the bill cannot be referred to the committee without prior endorsation of the principle which it involves. On principle, quite apart from defects in detail, it is unsound and should be defeated.
Several points of principle may be noted as follows:
1.	The bill would attempt to freeze, as of October 1, the percentage of shipments to be made by different elevators during the following year, and consequently the percentage of grain that each elevator at a given shipping point might expect to receive. That is to destroy competition in service. Nothing could be more contrary to the spirit of the Canada Grain Act, which endeavours to promote competition. Nothing could be more contrary to the basic philosophy which has animated parliament in the past and the major parties represented herein. At least it is contrary to the philosophy of the Liberal party. It may be that the C.C.F. party has adopted a philosophy to the effect that competition is undesirable and should be restrained.
2.	The proposal would discourage and even prevent elevator construction. There would be no incentive to build additional space if car allocation is frozen according to a predetermined cycle. This is in contrast with the present policy of the government, which is to encourage elevator construction by allowing accelerated write-off of capital costs.
3.	The proposal is in direct conflict with the Canadian Wheat Board Act, section 20(k), which gives the Canadian wheat board jurisdiction over allocation of box cars which
50433-237$
Canada Grain Act
are not placed pursuant to a car order book. Surely parliament cannot be expected to deprive the Canadian wheat board of powers which have previously been considered necessary for the purposes of that body.
4.	The proposal would hamper railway operation by introducing inefficiencies. It would frequently force cars to be placed at elevators in no position to make immediate use of them. The elevator may not contain grain of the type currently authorized for shipment by the Canadian wheat board. Or shipments from that particular elevator may be precluded because the operating company has elsewhere exhausted its current quota of authorized shipments.
5.	This and similar proposals have been based upon two misconceptions. One is to the effect that under present conditions each elevator in western Canada is afforded the same opportunity as its competitors to ship grain, because of an equal division of box cars, depending upon the will of the railway company. This idea is completely wrong. Take at random 50 points in Saskatchewan with two or more elevators, and you will probably find 50 elevators which have handled and shipped more grain than their competitors. Naturally so, for those with greater patronage or larger facilities are likely to have more grain of the types which the Canadian wheat board authorizes for shipment. Or again you may find that an elevator company has deliberately chosen to ship less of its authorized quota from one point in order, for some reason or other, to be able to ship more of its authorized quota from some other point.
6.	The other misconception is that there is a scarcity of box cars for grain shipment. On the contrary, the railways could supply many more cars to be loaded if there were any place to unload them. It is not the supply of box cars to country elevators which needs regulation. It is the unloading of grain into terminal elevators, something the Canadian wheat board is now regulating according to its best judgment. It strives to make the best possible use of terminal space; to keep flowing the kinds and grades of grain in current demand; to keep the pipe lines of supply from being clogged by grain of grades currently unsaleable. To do its work properly it must have freedom of action; it must not be hampered by any such rigid scheme of car allocation as this bill proposes.
7.	The Canadian wheat board, in authorizing shipments from the country, does so very largely on the basis of giving a quota to each elevator company. Each such company is then left as free as prevailing conditions permit to choose the point of origin of its

Canada Grain Act
shipments, with due regard to types of grain required and to areas most in need of relief. When the whole elevator system is congested with more grain than can be promptly disposed of, no system of controlling shipments can give perfect satisfaction at all times, to everyone and in every place. But certainly the flexible system now operated by the Canadian wheat board holds greater possibilities of fairness, of satisfaction and of efficiency than any scheme that has been proposed for interfering with the handling machinery along the lines of this bill.
8.	If this bill had any desirable features it would become necessary to consider another problem, whether or not it would be constitutional and within the competence of parliament. The government has been advised to the contrary, not indeed with respect to this particular bill but with respect to other proposals for allocation of box cars which would govern competition between elevator companies. But there is no need for legal argument in this connection, or of any reference to the supreme court, since the bill is undesirable of itself, quite apart from any question of constitutional validity.
This question has been discussed with the grain companies, and particularly with the farmer-owned companies. There is, in fact, a very sharp division among farmer-owned grain companies as to whether or not any plan of the kind suggested by the bill is desirable. I may say there has been no division of opinion about the merits of this bill, because it is the unanimous view of all grain companies, including all farmer-owned grain companies, that this bill is unworkable. However, the idea of farmers' preference has been to the fore recently, and a number of discussions have been held by myself and my officials with grain companies, particularly with farmer-owned grain companies.
The farmer-owned grain companies have themselves not been able to produce a bill which they would be prepared to support. I have never received a draft of such a bill, and my officers have been told by the solicitor of one of the companies that he had been unable to draft such a bill.
The whole idea of fixing a method of distribution of box cars for all time is completely mistaken, because conditions change from time to time. It was only two years ago that the transport controller received a letter signed jointly by the Alberta wheat pool, Mr. A. T. Baker, manager; North-West Line Elevators' Association, Alberta division, Mr. E. I. Ward, [DOT]chairman; and the United Grain Growers Liimited, Mr. W. J. Garland, superintendent of

elevators, which in effect asked that the principle of one car per elevator be reinstated. Perhaps I should read the letter; it might be interesting.

The key paragraph in this letter is:
Whereas the operation of car order books is not feasible under existing conditions and in any case is likely to favour the larger producer to the disadvantage of the small producer, it has been mutually agreed by all Alberta operators that,

during the 1953-54 crop year, temporary inequalities of distribution resulting from preferenced shipments shall be evened up at the earliest opportunity.
That was the situation that seemed desirable in Alberta for the crop of 1953-54, by unanimous consent of all the grain companies operating in that province. It may very well be the situation that the grain companies in that province would prefer in 1957-58.
The acute congestion seems to be passing; at least there is less congestion now than there has been for some years. Why, during a period of temporary congestion, attempt to freeze a system that may be wholly inapplicable for a period when no such congestion exists? That, I think, will appeal to every hon. member as not desirable, in the long-run interests of the producer in western Canada.
I do not think I need say more. I am perfectly sure that this bill, if enacted, would disorganize grain handling in western Canada to an extent that would tend to frustrate the efforts of all those who are attempting to do an efficient job of marketing the western producers grain.
We must have flexibility in the operation of country elevators and in the handling of stocks of grain contained in those elevators. It is true that when great quantities of grain were being handled the percentage of the Saskatchewan pool dropped several points from the percentage handled before congestion occurred. An effort is being made to reverse that trend, and I think the results of the current year will indicate that considerable progress has been made in that direction.
On the other hand, the percentage handled by the pool in Manitoba has not changed materially during the period of congestion. That is more or less true in Alberta, though I believe there has been some dropping off there.
Grain marketing in western Canada has been carried on under great difficulties. We have tried to handle five normal crops in a period of three years. The fact that there has not been greater dislocation is, I think, a credit to everyone concerned with the marketing of the western crop. I assure you that the efforts of all concerned are to give the greatest equality of marketing opportunity possible to producers in all parts of western Canada. I suggest that until some more perfect system is evolved than that provided for in this bill, parliament will be well advised to take no action in the matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
The
Minister of Trade and Commerce has indicated that the bill we have before us is
Canada Grain Act
tending to become a hardy perennial. I well remember the discussions on previous occasions when we had the bill before us, and I must say that only gradually has the significance of the problem impressed itself upon me.
The bill attempts to deal with the problem of grain distribution that has resulted from the congestion of the past three years. That problem has been concentrated largely in the province of Saskatchewan, with the result that Manitoba farmers have not been too concerned with the difficulties. For example, when we were discussing this matter of box car allocation in the agriculture committee last year I recall that the Manitoba representative of the pool elevator system disagreed with the representatives from Saskatchewan and Alberta. The position he took at that time arose from the fact that in Manitoba we were not faced to nearly the same extent with this problem of congestion. Since the meeting of the agriculture committee there has been a slight change in the attitude of the Manitoba farmers, particularly those doing business with the pool elevator system.
Just a few weeks ago I received a pamphlet dealing with this problem of box car allocation which puts forward in strong terms the necessity for a more equitable distribution. I note that this is endorsed by the three systems, the Manitoba pool elevators, the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the Alberta wheat pool which suggests to me that there is a change in thinking on this important subject.
For the first time I have been receiving letters on this matter. There was no ripple of concern at all in my constituency in the southwestern corner of Manitoba until the present year. I am interested to note that the aspect of the difficulty which is being protested against more than any other is in relation to those instances where you have the one for one distribution of box cars, that is, the formula where you have box cars spotted on the basis of one per elevator regardless of the normal pattern of grain business at any particular' elevator point.
During the Easter recess I took the trouble to do some personal investigating in connection with this matter. Certain letters had come to me, and I went out to interview the farmers who had submitted those letters.
I found that they had not any clear-cut thinking on a possible solution, but they certainly were unhappy because they could not do business with the elevator of their own choice. I discussed the bill which we have before us, but they were not personally acquainted with its provisions. If they were

Canada Grain Act
familiar with its contents these would be more or less incomprehensible to them, as are the contents of most bills that come before this house, which are drawn up in legal terminology. The result is that they generally remain an obscure issue with the layman.
I can say frankly that there does not seem to be any general support for the solution of the box car allocation problem presented in Bill No. 22. The reason I rose to take part in this discussion was to indicate dissatisfaction over the present state of affairs. I am inclined to agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there is no simple solution to the problem, nor will there be so long as the present congestion continues. We discussed this matter last year in the agriculture committee and there is to be another meeting of this committee within the next few days. I recommend strongly that we be given an opportunity to discuss this matter thoroughly in the committee.
The pool organizations have worked out an outline of a possible solution to the problem, and have placed this in the hands of certain hon. members. I received this outline with a covering letter from the Saskatchewan wheat pool over the signature of Mr. Robertson, the secretary. In this letter he stated:
The three pool organizations have been working together on this matter for some time. An interprovincial committee, composed of the vice presidents of the three pool organizations, has on various occasions been in touch with a member of the government in an effort to secure adequate amending legislation to meet the situation.
Mr. Robertson goes on to state that the representative of the interprovincial pool committee from the Manitoba pool is Mr. George McConnell, vice president of that organization. They have made some suggestions as to possible solutions of this box car allocation problem which are much more comprehensive than the provisions of the bill before us. I would like to indicate what those suggestions are.
In order to establish a workable basis for individual farmers, to deliver grain to elevators of their own choice, certain amendments would be required to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and also to the Canada Grain Act. It is suggested, first, that a provision be inserted in the wheat board act whereby the wheat board would furnish yearly to the board of grain commissioners a list of growers who had delivered grain the previous year, together with their address and seeded acreage.
Second, that a provision be inserted in the Canada Grain Act to authorize the board of grain commissioners to send yearly to every such grower a form to be completed and

returned stating his delivery preference; with this information the board of grain commissioners to determine a cycle of car distribution for each point, and to inform the appropriate elevator companies and the railways of such cycle.
Third, cars ordered within the period by the wheat board to be treated as part of the cycle.
Fourth, cars spotted but not loaded by the elevator company to be treated as part of its cycle.
Fifth, all grain in store in country elevators at the time the cycle comes into operation to come under its jurisdiction.
Sixth, the board of grain commissioners should also be authorized to make whatever regulations are required to enable any cycle to operate successfully.
That is a much more comprehensive treatment of the matter than we have in the bill before us. Certain local elevator operators have indicated to me that the ideal solution would be to have the local railway agent allocate cars according to his understanding of the local delivery situation. But it has also been indicated to me that the local railway agents are unwilling to take such responsibility, and I have a reply from the local agent at Fairfax, Manitoba, substantiating this. It was indicated to me that the agent answered that he could do nothing about it at all and quoted the grain act, the transport controller, the car order book regulations, etc. This letter from the secretary of the Fairfax co-operative elevator goes on to state:
If he is correct, which we doubt, then why are laws not altered or clarified to bring this business up to date with the situations of today.
The local railway agent did not want to assume this responsibility because of the difficulties he would encounter in relation to the transport controller, the Canada Grain Act, etc.
Now, Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I cannot agree that this bill would solve the problem, because it introduces further rigidity into a system that is already too rigid under circumstances of congestion. The sponsor of the bill made a moving plea in his initial statement for greater flexibility in handling the movement of grain. He made a stirring plea that the processes of free competition and free enterprise might be allowed to operate among our farming community. That immediately put me on my guard, coming from that particular source; and I am afraid that if he is sincere in his advocacy of that particular viewpoint, I must conclude that this bill would not solve the problem.

I would repeat in closing that there is a growing demand from the farming community that something be done so the individual farmer is placed in a position where he may deliver his grain to the elevator of his choice. That demand will continue so long as the prevailing congestion is with us, and I would very strongly recommend that we take an opportunity to discuss this matter again in the agriculture committee. The pamphlet that has been sponsored by the pool elevator associations of the three prairie provinces would indicate that there is a change in the thinking of the Manitoba pool organization on this matter. I would certainly appreciate having the opportunity to consider this matter in broad perspective, and not confined as it is here to the relatively restricted terms of this Bill No. 22.
