speechtext:
The principle of this bill is set out very clearly in the explanatory notes. I think it would be well to have it on the record again because of some of the things that have been said this afternoon and on the last occasion it was before the house. In the explanatory notes the principle is set out in these words:
The purpose of this act is to remove discrimination in the allocation of box cars by providing in a new section of the car order book a rule for the fair allocation of box cars among elevator companies at a marketing point where the car order book, as presently constituted, is not in effect. By allocating their seeded acreage among the elevator companies at a marketing point, producers themselves will determine the distribution of box cars at that point.
Canada Grain Act
I fail to see how anyone representing agriculture in this house could deny the value of that principle. Certainly, if the producers themselves wish to express a preference as to the elevator company with whom they want to do business, then they should be allowed to do so. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has opposed the bill, and strangely enough the basis of his opposition to the bill seemed to be that the philosophy behind it and behind the arguments used by members of this group has run counter to the philosophy of the Liberal party, which he states is competition. I am sure that statement will be examined with great interest by co-operators right across Canada, because now the minister has placed the Liberal party squarely on the side of competition and of course, by doing so, squarely against co-operation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext: That is nonsense.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
You cannot have it both ways, my friend. Mr. Speaker, I say that is a strange basis on which to oppose this legislation, because I have so often heard members of the Liberal party, from the prairies at least, attempt to take a great deal of credit for the setting up of the Canadian wheat board. What was the reason for the setting up of the Canadian wheat board in the first instance? It was exactly the same reasoning as was behind the setting up of the wheat pools and the co-operative handling of grain. It was a method of doing the marketing for the farmer in a co-operative manner rather than in a competitive manner.
Certainly if this philosophy expressed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce today on behalf of the Liberal party were followed to its logical conclusion it would mean the end of the wheat board entirely and a return to the old competitive system of the Winnipeg grain exchange. There is no other conclusion to which one may come. I would be very much surprised if the minister could persuade the grain producers of western Canada that it is a good thing for them to go back to a competitive position in the marketing of their grain.
Let us take, for example, a thousand farmers in a community. I am sure if the minister told them the best way they could market their grain was for each farmer to be always in competition with the 999 other farmers, we would hear some very interesting comments from the grain producers. We cannot get away from it. The line is very clearly drawn now. This group is trying to bring justice to the grain producers. We are squarely behind the co-operative principle, and we have no hesitation in saying

Supply-Northern Affairs so. I support the co-operative philosophy right down the line. The minister takes his party down the line of competition. Of course it will be up to the people to choose.

Mr. Chairman, just before five o'clock I had been quoting from an article by Mr. Turnbull, president of the Edmonton trout fishing club, and printed in "The Voice of Motordom", regarding what he considered the poor fishing facilities in the national parks of Banff and Jasper.
I have heard many reasons advanced why the fishing in those parks is of a somewhat poor character. I have been told by officials in the parks that it is largely owing to the fact that the water is too cold and greatly retards the growth of the fish. I have also been told that there is too much silt and that the silt affects the spawning. I have also been told that there is a lack of feed in many of the lakes. On the other hand many men who have had a great deal of experience in this matter in other national parks in other parts of the country feel that with a good program, with sufficient backing, it would be possible to greatly improve the situation.
In that same article Mr. Turnbull makes this comment:
If your provincial government can do this wonderful work of restocking with such success, others can do the same. General conditions are the same, invested facilities in the park such as hatcheries, etc., are possibly better; the only thing that seems to be wrong is lack of management and experience.
Then he goes on to give the names of a number of men living in Jasper who he feels could give the government valuable assistance in helping to improve the situation. But personally I do not doubt for one minute that

the department has men who are just as good and who know just as much about the question of improving fishing conditions as anyone else. Provided they were given sufficient backing, they could no doubt take care of the situation.
It is interesting to note the program that has been carried on of recent years in Alberta. There was a time when it was practically impossible to get trout fishing on the prairies, but today we find that there is great trout fishing in many parts of Alberta as a result of the new program, and that is so in spots similar in character to the park because they are in the mountains alongside the park.
I just want to read one or two quotations from "Within Our Borders" dealing with this question. The heading is "Large Trout Await Anglers in Small Alberta Lakes" and the article goes on to say:
Small lakes In Alberta are providing an overabundance of trout fishing to such a point that the fisheries branch of the lands and forests department has had to appeal to anglers to fish the small lakes heavily.
I hope the day will come when the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources will also have to give that advice to people in the national parks. The article continues:
Alberta fishery officers, looking for new places to plant trout where they would provide more and better fishing for the average fisherman, tried stocking prairie potholes which had no fish at all.
I would suggest to the minister that he might suggest to the provincial government of Alberta that if they have any surplus fish they might put them in some of the lakes in the national parks. The article continues:
Because the lakes offer no facilities for spawning, regular restocking is necessary but before new fish can be planted, they must be fished out. The reason for this is that after the third summer the original fish stocked have grown so large that they dominate the lakes and their food supply, leaving no room for young fish.
Alberta fishery officials have found that lakes with surface areas of between 80 and 200 acres are ideal for rainbow stocking. They can be stocked economically and are small enough to be fished out in time to allow a second planting of trout.
If subsequent fish planted in the lakes are to survive, the previous fish must be all caught by the fourth summer from the time of stocking. If some of the originals remain, they have to be removed before new stock can be introduced to the lakes.
It is extremely interesting to note what has been done in that regard, and as a result we have this peculiar situation. We find that a number of the people living in Banff, which is looked upon by many people as a fisherman's paradise, when they want to go fishing go outside the park, either into Alberta or

British Columbia, in order to get fishing. I think it should be possible to improve the fishing in a number of the lakes by a greater program of restocking.
It is interesting to note that a few years ago certain parties in Banff asked permission to start a trout farm in the park. The former minister was greatly interested in that offer and he said he knew of a similar program in Nova Scotia which had been quite a success. At that time he seemed quite keen on the idea of allowing a trout farm to be instituted in Banff. But unfortunately his officials apparently had an entirely different view. They frowned upon the suggestion and drew up a number of requirements that had to be met before permission would be granted. All those requirements were fulfilled, yet in spite of that fact the plan was stalled and I suppose today the whole thing has been given up. I have not heard any more about it lately.
I quite agree that the type of fishing that would be provided by a trout farm would not be in the same class as that provided in the natural form. I think we would all much prefer to do our fishing in a natural stream or a natural lake rather than go to a trout farm for our fishing. On the other hand many families who go into Banff park are not in a position to wander up the streams for many miles. They have their children with them. To them it would be a great thing if they could go to a trout farm, fish and catch a few trout.
As I say, I do not think anything can compare with the joy of going up into the mountains, amongst the fine scenery, in the fine mountain air, to do some fishing. There is only one thing lacking in so far as Banff is concerned, namely fish. And after all, if you are going fishing you need some fish.
I am not suggesting there are no fish in Banff. We all know there are many places in Banff where there is very good fishing; but those points are a number of miles from the highway and, as I say, it is not possible for many people to enjoy that type of fishing. It generally requires equipment which is beyond the means of certain people, or maybe they have not the time to wander 15 miles or so off the beaten track. I therefore hope the minister will give careful consideration to a program of improving the fishing in the natural lakes.
I have met a number of Americans in Banff who have just been boiling mad. They received certain circulars about our wonderful fishing, and how our streams are teeming with fish. I met an American in the store one day. I was in there buying black gnats.
Supply-Northern Affairs He said, "There is no use buying those. I have over $1,000 worth of fishing gear, and I have not caught a fish yet."

speechtext: You do not think he is alone, do you?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No, he is not alone by any means. There are many of them. Again I will frankly admit that there are spots in Banff where there is good fishing, provided you have the time and the inclination to walk far enough to reach them. But in the lakes that are easily accessible the fishing, generally speaking, is very poor.

That is true in a way. I have seen little boys, fishing in the Bow river with a worm and small hook, pull out fish; but they are generally small fish. A grown-up would probably throw the fish back because it would be below legal size. But being little boys they pop them in their pockets and go off home with them.
I have fished with practically everything you can think of, including dry flies, wet flies, nymphs, spinners, gentles, and anything else you like. I have even resorted to worms when I have been desperate; but even so, I found it rather hard to catch fish. I think I am what you might call an average fisherman. I do not claim to be a good one. I have caught plenty of trout in Banff, but the hours I spent in doing so were quite numerous. I have averaged about three hours for every fish I caught. I kept track of them, because in Banff they are very keen about having you fill in creel cards.
When you go fishing they tell you to fill in a creel card. First of all, I found that if I went to the repository for a creel card, as a rule there would be no cards there. Then by the time I got home I would forget to note down all the information. I notice in the creel card reports the time spent catching fish is tabulated, and the average would appear to be three-quarters of an hour or one hour per fish depending on the location. That information is not very accurate because people who go there and fish for hours and do not catch any fish do not bother as a rule to fill out a card. Consequently the reports do not give a very accurate picture of the situation.
There is one other suggestion I should like to make to the minister. The department should bring the "Anglers' Guide" up to date. I notice in that guide there is quite a bit of information that is very much out of date. For instance, they talk about crossing Massive bridge. Massive bridge went out several

Supply-Northern Affairs years ago. There is no bridge there; yet the most recent issue still tells you to cross Massive bridge. There is no bridge to cross unless you can jump across a space of about 30 feet where two spans are missing.
That is all I have to say. I hope the minister will give the matter careful consideration. I know it is not the first time he has been approached about it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened to the hon. member for Acadia, and all I can say is that the people in his part of the country had better come to New Brunswick national park, where they will really get some fishing. They will not have to fish for a week without any success, because we have some very good trout in our national park, both in the lake and in the different streams.
I do not intend to discuss that phase of our national park tonight. Ours is one of the newest national parks in Canada, if not the newest, and we are very proud of it. It was a very large undertaking and has been most successful. There were many roads and camps to be built. So far as recreation is concerned, there is a fine golf course and there are large picnic grounds. Every year the number of people visiting Fundy national park in New Brunswick is increasing.
We in New Brunswick feel that the man who was largely responsible for the excellent job that has been done there was the superintendent, Mr. Saunders, who was appointed a few years ago on the recommendation of Mr. McNair, I believe, who was then premier of New Brunswick. At the present time the people of New Brunswick, particularly those who are interested in the national park-and we all are-are quite concerned because they understand the superintendent is either to be retired or transferred to some other national park. I should like to ask the minister tonight what is the policy of the department with reference to the transferring of superintendents from one national park to another, why they feel it is necessary to make these transfers, and also what the policy is with reference to the retirement of superintendents of national parks.
I understand our superintendent was advised nearly a year ago that he was going to be transferred to a national park in Manitoba. He is a man about 59 years of age, and has given splendid service in the province of New Brunswick. He understands our situation there as no other man does, and there must be enormous expense involved in transferring a man with all his household effects from New Brunswick to Manitoba and transferring the Manitoba superintendent to the national park in New Brunswick. It seems to

me a poor policy, and one which does not mean any betterment as far as the superintendents are concerned.
I hope the minister will be able to explain this matter satisfactorily because, as I say, the people of New Brunswick are quite concerned. Up until a little over a year ago there was no suggestion whatever of transferring the superintendent of the national park in New Brunswick to any other place, nor any suggestion of his retirement. Mr. Saunders has taken a very active part in the public life of his community. He has been active on practically all committees having anything to do with the betterment of the community, and a little over a year ago he was asked if he would run for the position of councillor in the parish of Alma in the county of Albert, where the park is located.
It may have been and probably was indiscreet on the part of the superintendent to take part in any kind of election, even a council election which is not supposed to be political in any sense of the word. Mr. Saunders allowed himself to be persuaded to run for councillor. He ran against a man who had been in office for a number of years and gave him a trimming. Shortly after Mr. Saunders was notified that he would be transferred to another park. The man he defeated in the election was chairman of the government organization in that particular part of Albert county, and is also a great friend of the former member for Saint John-Albert. The minister shakes his head. I am simply stating what the people in that section of the county and in New Brunswick generally feel. It is their opinion that this man was told he would be transferred to another national park simply because he ran for a council seat in this particular parish.
I hope the minister has a satisfactory explanation tonight, because we are concerned. Here we have had an excellent superintendent for our national park, a man who has given us one of the finest national parks in Canada, and at the age of 59 he is notified that he is to be transferred to Manitoba, that he and his family must take up their roots and go to another part of Canada. He has refused to be transferred to Manitoba, and now he is being retired at the age of 59. I understand his pension is going to be much less than it would be if he had been able to serve his full time.
I have met Mr. Saunders once, but he has never communicated with me in any way. I am simply giving expression tonight to the opinion of many people in my own town of Sussex, which is near the national park, people in the county of Albert and throughout New Brunswick who feel that a great

injustice has been done to a very fine public servant, a man who has given to this national park the very best he had to give. I hope the minister will be able to give a satisfactory explanation and will be able to say to me tonight that no injustice will be done to this man who, I believe, is being asked to retire before he has earned and can be paid the full amount of his retirement allowance.

May I give my explanation, Mr. Chairman? I believe I have let the hon. member for Royal make his statement without interruption. May I say again that this

Supply-Northern Affairs department is not retiring Mr. Saunders. Mr. Saunders chose to offer his resignation when he was told that he would be transferred. Rather than be transferred he answered that he wished to retire at the age of 60, and his resignation was accepted. He will get his civil service pension.
May I quote the policy of the department as set out in the committee proceedings, and as I explained it when there was no question about Mr. Saunders. I am reading from page 638 of the estimates committee report:
I believe it is a good thing to move superintendents around every five years or so for the following reasons: First, the superintendents will have gathered experience and they will go to a park with new ideas for that park. Secondly, psychologically when a man comes into a new post he will be wanting to make a good job of it. But after five, six, seven or eight years he might settle down and we are afraid he will lack imagination . . .

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: When you stay five years-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Five years or more.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I would be inclined to agree because I would not look on five years as being a frequent move.
When Mr. Saunders was told that he would be transferred in accordance with the policy of the department-it had been the policy before I became minister-he decided to retire. My predecessor in office, who is behind me now, is telling me that was his policy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: How many have been transferred, may I ask?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Since 1953 there have been' five transferred, out of a total of 16 park superintendents.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What were their ages?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Age has nothing to do with it. We transfer them every five or six years. A man of 59 still has six years left, and the intention was to move superintendent Bryant from Kootenay park to Fundy and to move superintendent Saunders to Kootenay park.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What was the date of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The decision was in March, 1954. My predecessor just tells me-I came into the department in the fall of 1953- that there had been a question about moving Mr. Saunders before I came into the department, so it was not new. That was in accordance with departmental policy. No wrong has been done to Mr. Saunders. On the contrary, rather than be transferred he decided on his own to offer his resignation and take his pension. There is no injustice to Mr. Saunders.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have no desire to detain the committee for very long. I wish to tell the minister that the Lethbridge federal riding thinks he is doing an exceedingly good

Supply-Northern Affairs job. They greatly appreciated having him come out and visit them last year. They were delighted with the impression he made, and with the fact that he seemed to have learned everything there was to be known about Waterton Lakes park in the short time he was there. He seemed to fit right into the scheme of things. We bid him welcome any time he chooses to visit us.
We believe also that the progress that has been made during the last two or three years in connection with the park is satisfactory. I should like to take this opportunity of thanking the present Minister of Public Works, who was the predecessor of the present minister of northern affairs, for appointing to Waterton Lakes park as superintendent Mr. J. H. Atkinson. I think Mr. Atkinson's coming was the greatest blessing that ever happened to the park. I would be pleased to have the present minister forget to transfer Mr. Atkinson when his five or so years are up. Just let him stay on there, because he seems to fit into that park almost as well as the Waterton lakes do.
We feel that the amount of money that has been expended on the park this year is quite satisfactory. Indeed, we can understand that in a year in which the government has felt it necessary to save a little bit more money than they have in times past, they appropriated as much as seemed fitting under the circumstances.
We would like, however, to have more money next year, and for this reason. We feel that one of the essentials in making Waterton Lakes park the dream park which we all, including the minister, wish it to be, would be a fine swimming pool in the park. This should not be a swimming pool alone, but a building in which people could take refuge in case of stormy, windy, cold or wet weather which sometimes comes to that part for two or three days. We believe that a fine building, erected as an attraction both winter and summer to house a swimming pool, would be so great an asset to that park that the necessary money, probably $300,000 or $400,000, would be money exceedingly well spent. We would ask the minister to do all he possibly can to impress the treasury board with the idea that they should extend themselves a little for a year or two while they build that swimming pool.
I think nothing more needs to be said, except to report to the minister that, so far as 1 know, everything in Waterton Lakes park is going along as well as could be expected. We are just waiting for the days to come and go while we grow in Waterton Lakes park. While I do not propose to contest
[Mr. Blackmore.i
what the hon. member for Bow River and several others have said about their respective parks being the very best, I would probably question the standard by which they judge parks.
In closing I would point out that Waterton Lakes park is of exceptional importance because it is the front window of Canada in that particular area. It is right down against Glacier national park, being located at the extreme southwest corner of Alberta. It is the park to which United States tourists come to get an impression of Canada, which impression will cause them either to go far into the interior, away into the northland, or turn around and go back. We all want them to go far into the interior, away into the northland. We say, therefore, let us pay particular attention to making Waterton Lakes the very finest park in Canada, whether or not it is so now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to once again raise a matter I mentioned in this house a year ago. I noticed that after the last session the minister spent some time in making a number of visits to some of our national parks. I should like to recommend that the next time he comes to British Columbia he pay a call on the minister of fisheries there and ask that minister to take him on a tour of a provincial park. He will probably have to go by saddle horse. I am referring, of course, to Garibaldi provincial park, which I feel is a park that, once developed, would be Canada's leading national park.
Last year I asked the minister about this, and he expressed the interest of his department in taking over from the provincial government the responsibility for the development of Garibaldi park. The minister stated some conditions that would have to be met before his department could consider taking it over. One condition was that a first-class highway be constructed to the entrance of the park. We have a first-class highway, the Lougheed highway, that runs to within two or three miles of the southern entrance to Garibaldi. I think the minister had in mind at that time a first-class highway that would give access to the northern entrance. I understand that the government of British Columbia is now proceeding with the Howe Sound highway, and this highway, when completed, will give access to the northern entrance of the park. Therefore that condition is being met.
The other condition mentioned was that the provincial government be prepared to hand over all interest in the park, and this would include all interest in the mineral

resources. 1 understand that former governments of British Columbia-not the present government-when considering this matter always hesitated to hand over the mineral rights to the federal government. There was the feeling that possibly they were handing over to a higher level of government untold millions of dollars by way of future mineral royalties.
As one of the daily newspapers pointed out only some six months ago, this would be a very shortsighted policy for the government of British Columbia to adopt. While 50 years from now they might obtain $10 million, $15 million, or even $20 million in royalties from minerals that might be found at that time, in the meantime the provincial coffers were annually losing untold millions of dollars from tourists who would visit this park if the development were begun now. I hope that attitude of former governments of British Columbia is not being adopted by the government we now have in British Columbia. I hope the minister will be able to report some progress in the negotiations, or at least be able to report that over the past year he has commenced negotiations.
I would not like him to think he has to leave the initiation of such negotiations to the provincial government. The development of Garibaldi park is beyond the resources of the government of British Columbia. We cannot begin to develop Garibaldi park for less than $30 million, and the government of British Columbia simply is not in a position to begin spending that kind of money on one item. It would be in the national interest to develop this park. I say this, and I have endorsation of it in statements made on other occasions in other places by the Minister of Fisheries. Garibaldi park has the potential to become one of the most famous parks not only of Canada but of the whole world. I believe the Minister of Fisheries is responsible for saying that while he had looked at practically all of the world's famous ski resorts, not one of them, even those in the Alps mountains, would be able to hold up against this park in British Columbia if it were developed.
One of the first things necessary for that development, of course, would be a highway from the southern end right through the park to the northern end, and that is where many millions of dollars enter the picture. It is possible that a bridge would also have to be constructed across the Fraser river at Haney to handle the tourist traffic we would be sure to have from the south.
I would also very much like to see Garibaldi park developed as a national park soon.
Supply-Northern Affairs I am not opposed to, and I endorse, the development of the national parks we now have in Canada, and I would like to see even more developed, but in the lower mainland most of our people live within a hundred miles of the city of Vancouver. Out of a population of 1,250,000 people in the province, some 750,000 live within a hundred miles of Vancouver. These people have only limited park facilities available to them. On Sunday about the only place they can go is to Stanley park; and if you visit Stanley park on a Sunday afternoon you find the place is literally crowded with people. It has reached the stage that if you want to relax in Stanley park you have to go there on a Monday or a Tuesday, when most people are at work. It is urgent that we have park facilities available offering fairly easy access to the 750,00Q people.
It is all very well to say that British Columbia has national parks. The national parks in British Columbia are hundreds of miles removed from where most of the people live. In our lower mainland area we have tens of thousands of people who have no means of transportation available. These people receive absolutely no advantage from the development of our national parks that are away off in the Rocky mountains. It is on behalf of those people in the lower mainland who need the park, who have not the wherewithal to spend several weeks hundreds of miles away from home, who would be glad to make use of public transportation facilities at a cost of 75 cents or a dollar, that I speak. It could become one of the most wonderful playgrounds of the Dominion of Canada.
On behalf of these three-quarters of a million taxpayers of Canada, I urge that further negotiations should take place. If the negotiations have not yet begun I hope they definitely will begin, and that this government will not wait for the government of British Columbia to take the initiative in this matter.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
300. Grant in aid of the development of the international peace garden in Manitoba, $10,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I hear groans coming from the backbenchers, but I assure the groaners that I shall not carry on at any great length with this subject. I mentioned this topic during the discussion in the committee on estimates. The only reason I raise it now is that I know the minister would be disappointed if I did not make some reference to it, and I know that at least the chairman also would be disappointed, because he is one of those fortunate men who had the opportunity during the past summer to visit

Supply-Northern Affairs the international peace garden on the Manitoba-North Dakota boundary.
I want to express appreciation to the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources for continuing this $10,000 grant in aid of the development of the international peace garden, which began as a voluntary effort on the part of the peoples of Canada and the United States to symbolize the universal desire for peace. The cairn marking the spot, which was dedicated in 1932, is inscribed as follows:
To God in His Glory
We two nations dedicate this garden and pledge ourselves that as long as men shall live, we will not take up arms against one another.
I should point out that the garden which began as a symbol of the universal desire for peace has now developed into one of the outstanding tourist attractions in the midcontinental area of North America. I have often heard travellers in Canada say they like to visit the scenic spots in the Rocky mountain district or that they enjoy travelling in Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes, but they indicate they are not too inspired with our flat, level prairies in the centre part of the country.
Here is a development which has offset that vacuum in tourist attractions which has existed in the centre of our country. Not only from the standpoint of its own scenic beauty but also from the standpoint of its symbolic appeal is it drawing increasingly large numbers of tourists. Although this is not a part of our system of national parks it certainly can be regarded as an extension.
I would venture to say that the fact Riding Mountain national park attracted 500,000 visitors last year was due in large part to the visitors who were interested in the international peace garden and then continued on some hundred miles further north to the Riding Mountain national park.
In reality the international peace garden is an international park and today it is creating world-wide interest. It is because of this growing interest that I venture to say a few words tonight so the matter may be kept before hon. members of this house and the people of Canada as a whole.
As I have indicated, this is a co-operative effort by the peoples of Canada and the United States. I should like to compare the support we are giving this garden to that given by the United States. Their grant amounts to $100,000 for a period of three years, which means that they are providing $33,000 per annum as against our $10,000. As indicative of the significance of this international peace garden I might say that the
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
state of North Dakota is adding to its automobile licence plates the phrase "the peace garden state". That form of publicity will go a long way in popularizing the development among the peoples of North Dakota and the United States as a whole.
One further comment on this item. I notice that the grant for the national battlefields commission is being increased from $100,000 to $125,000 and also that the grant to provide for special work at national battlefields park, Quebec, is being increased from $6,000 to $8,000. Just in case they have forgotten, I should like to remind hon. members of the committee that up until three years ago the annual grant to the international peace garden was $15,000. Then it disappeared for a year and was restored at the reduced rate of $10,000 per annum. As an investment in the cause of peace I believe this development is unparalleled. Moreover, I should like to emphasize that every dollar expended in the development of the garden will be returned in manifold ways because of its powerful attraction as a tourist centre.
It is my belief that in the not too far distant future we shall see the United States establishing a suitable building as a museum on their side of the garden area. The question of making the international peace garden a national arboretum is under consideration, and inevitably Canada will be forced to think along the same lines if this development continues to capture the imagination of people on both sides of the border as well as people throughout the world.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to back up what the hon. member for Brandon-Souris has said. I lived in Souris for six years, and those with whom I was associated were intensely interested in this park. The latest report I have had is that the superintendent of the park treats the tourists so well that they want to come back again.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in support of what the hon. member for Brandon-Souris has said. This is one time when I can support a proposal of my hon. friend, and I do it with a great deal of pleasure. The hon. member has covered the history and background of this worthy project, and I would like to ask the minister to consider increasing the grant. As has been pointed out, the United States grant is $100,000 for three years, whereas ours is $10,000 a year. I believe the grant should be doubled, not only from the tourist attraction standpoint but because of the great work that has been done in this international peace garden.

I am not going to repeat what the hon. member for Brandon-Souris has said, but I should like to quote the last paragraph of this pamphlet giving the history and progress of the international peace garden, this being the revised edition for 1953. It reads:
Perhaps the most encouraging aspect of the year has been the realization of internationalism in the garden. Not only has there been over three times the number of visitors of the previous year, but they have come from 48 states and 10 provinces on this continent, and nine countries of the world beyond. In June, there was a pilgrimage of the National Council of Women of Canada, during their convention, to the garden; and in the fall, the Associated Countrywomen of the World sent delegates from many countries to the garden. An international relations conference of students from the Minot state college of North Dakota and the students of Brandon college, Brandon, Manitoba, added further significance to the garden; while the annual meeting of the garden itself in early September forms the focal point of the year's work. Through the international addresses of prominent people of both countries at this time the citizens get the "timeless vision that peace is something to cherish, that it is something one has to work for, and that here people are working to erect not statues and memorials to commemorate victory in war or valor in combat, but instead a lovely garden to honor and laud peace itself."
For that reason alone, if for no other, we should make a little greater contribution than in the past.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, just to make it unanimous may I join with my friends from the province of Manitoba in supporting the expressions of appreciation and the appeals they have made. I am very glad this grant was restored a year or two ago. In my view those who preceded me are perfectly right in their suggestion that we might well increase the amount of the grant to the international peace garden.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
303. Canadian wildlife service-wildlife resources conservation and development, including administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, $455,703.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to make a few observations on this item. Before going on to the particular matter which I rose to mention, I wish to say that I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Acadia, and after listening to him I can fully appreciate now why he is called the Izaak Walton of the Social Credit party. I suggest to the member that it would be much less expensive to visit Kootenay West if he wants to catch some fish, rather than to spend all that money in the area the hon. member mentioned.
However, the hon. member for The Battle-fords was called away unexpectedly this afternoon and he asked me to bring to the minister's attention something of particular interest to some of his constituents as well
Supply-Northern Affairs as persons in other parts of Canada. He has received representations from various people protesting the use of steel traps in the Northwest Territories. The argument in favour of these representations by these people is that, while we live in a Christian civilization, we still promote primitive and cruel methods of trapping, particularly the use of steel traps in the Northwest Territories.
I am informed that, owing to the length of the trap lines, the traps are frequently not emptied for a month at a time. Naturally this causes days of suffering and a great deal of misery to the fur-bearing animals. They slowly die from their injuries or from starvation in the cold. The hon. member has asked me to bring to the minister's attention the fact that the law in the United States at the present time requires that every trap in a registered trap line must be visited at least once every 24 hours.
Anyone who understands anything about trapping-and I had a 15-mile trap line myself at one time-will realize that that is impossible. I am informed that in Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Germany steel traps for the trapping of fur-bearing animals are completely prohibited by law. They have replaced the system of steel traps. A more humane form of trap has been found quite satisfactory by the trappers in those countries.
The hon. member for The Battlefords brought to my attention, before he left this afternoon, that last year the Prime Minister of Canada sent a special message of best wishes to the Ottawa organization of the "Be Kind to Animals" week, and expressed his interest in the efforts of the organization to promote the humane treatment of animals. That is a clear indication that the Prime Minister of this country is very much interested in that question. I think you can relate the catching of fur-bearing animals with steel traps to that sort of approach to the question of the humane treatment of animals.
I realize all the difficulties connected with this problem. As I said before, I have done some trapping myself, and it is not so easy to find a replacement as one might imagine if one has had no experience in that line. But those making representations to the hon. member for The Battlefords suggest that the department would be well advised to investigate the methods used in other countries, particularly the countries I have mentioned, where they have completely abolished the use of steel traps for the catching of fur-bearing animals and now have a humane form of trap. The department could investigate the possibilities of replacing steel traps in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and, as

Supply-Northern Affairs they were gradually replaced, assisting the trappers to purchase the new form of humane trap by means of a subsidy after the fashion of the subsidy given to Quebec farmers to purchase aluminum pails for the gathering of sap.
I bring these matters to the attention of the minister at the request of the hon. member for The Battlefords. I suggest that the minister go into the whole question and have it investigated, and possibly set a target date for the elimination of the use of steel traps for the catching of fur-bearing animals, because of the cruelty involved therein.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Engineering and water resources branch-
305. Branch administration, $54,283.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I believe this is the point at which the hon. member for St. Paul's was told previously by the minister that he should bring up the matter about which he had begun to speak in connection with flood warnings. As he was unable to be here tonight he asked me to raise this matter.
The hon. member for St. Paul's is of the opinion that the great loss of life which occurred owing to "Hurricane Hazel" in and around the vicinity of Toronto could very well have been prevented if the people in those low-lying valleys had had a few hours' warning of what the height of water was likely to be as a result of the very heavy rains which had occurred. He was also of the opinion that this rainfall was known to the meteorological officers, and that warning could have been given. He asked me to take up the question with the minister as to whether any arrangements exist or have been put into effect since that time to give people warning of what height of flood water may be expected following a heavy storm.
We all know, of course, that once the water has fallen it takes a considerable length of time for the run-off to go down and reach an area such as that around Toronto where all this flooding took place. That provides sufficient time, as long as warning is given, for the people to evacuate any low-lying areas; or, if they are not willing to evacuate them, it gives sufficient time for the police to forcibly take them out of those areas, thus avoiding tragedies such as those which took place in the Toronto area.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the responsibilities and duties of the water resources division were explained at length in the committee, but I do not recall that that question of flood warning was raised there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: What was mentioned in the committee was that this department, through its water resources division, was co-operating with the provinces in collecting the readings and gauging the levels of the streams all the year round. We communicate to the provincial authorities the readings of the levels of the rivers at regular intervals and, when the water rises, communications are more frequent. As a matter of fact this is done regularly for the Columbia river, the Bow river, the Fraser river, the Assiniboine river and the Red river, among others, but in the case of the Humber river I would have to look into it to ascertain if we have gauging stations on that river. We have some gauging stations on the Humber, but there have never been any flood warning arrangements there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Might I ask the minister this question. In all those areas where they have these gauging stations and where there are low-lying river bottoms where possibly serious damage, serious loss of life and so forth could take place in the event of a flood, cannot a warning system be instituted in order to prevent this sort of thing in the future? I refer not just to Toronto but any place else in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I was just discussing that matter with my officials. We will look into the matter and will co-operate fully with the provinces so they may be advised constantly of the water levels, especially when they rise suddenly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to call the attention of the minister to the serious condition that exists in Saskatchewan and Manitoba as a result of the flooding of the Assiniboine river. The drainage basin of that river covers a large area, namely some 60,000 square miles. Owing to the fact that the river runs through a country with alluvial soil, it is subject to silting. As a consequence the river bottom has been rising and the river has been subjected to flooding almost yearly, of late years, with a great deal of damage to farm lands-

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I say that the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has no responsibility at all for flood damage. As I explained in the committee, the only responsibilities of the water resources branch, as far as rivers across the country are concerned and the levels of the rivers, are to study those levels by engineering surveys for development of the rivers and also, in cooperation with the provinces, to establish some gauging stations and to read the levels. The responsibility for flood prevention and

flood damage does not come under this department at all. There is no item which covers that matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not suggesting that the department assume any responsibility for flood damage. However, I am assuming that the department have a certain responsibility for flood control. The minister himself has indicated that they have some responsibility for surveys in co-operation with the provinces. I suggest that in these estimates there is an item indicating an expenditure for damage on the Conestogo river. How would the minister classify that expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This was for water conservation, under a special agreement that was made with the government of Ontario under which we provided 37J per cent of the cost. There is a special item for that expenditure in the estimates. This was not especially for flood control but for water conservation.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
The item referred to by the minister is item 310. I shall read it for his benefit:
To provide for a contribution to the cost of constructing a dam on the Conestogo river near Glen Allan, Ontario, for the purposes of flood control and water conservation, in accordance with the terms of an agreement entered into between Canada and the province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, but flood control is still a provincial responsibility. Unless we have a request from a provincial government for participation under the Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act there is no responsibility on the part of this department for flood control. The present situation on the Assini-boine river has nothing to do with this department, or I should say this department has nothing to do with the present situation on the Assiniboine river. That is better.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, there is a possibility that the provincial government might seek the assistance of the minister's department in the same way the government of Ontario sought it in connection with the Conestogo river.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: All right. When we have it we will consider it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Perhaps it would not be amiss if one might briefly state what P.F.R.A. have recommended.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the Department of Agriculture, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
One does not know whether the Department of Agriculture will do anything. They have made engineering surveys and a recommendation. But the Department
Supply-Northern Affairs of Agriculture are not doing anything. As a consequence, year by year the farmers in the Assiniboine river area are obliged to suffer this flood damage. This is costing them millions of dollars year by year.
I could, of course, take this matter up under the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, but I suggest that possibly the minister's department might collaborate with the Department of Agriculture or with the provincial government in some way, as was done in Ontario, so this condition could be ameliorated. However, if the minister does not want to hear such a recommendation I do not suppose I have any alternative but to desist.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the government at this time. I have reason to assume that it fits into this particular part of the debate. However, if I am out of order I am sure I shall soon be reminded about it.
The matter has to do with a situation existing on the Vedder river in British Columbia. In this connection I had submitted to me a brief containing letters starting at May 15, 1952 and bringing the matter right up to a very recent date. These communications are between Mr. Mulford, the clerk of the corporation of the township of Chilliwack and Mr. Cruickshank, a former member of parliament, and also between other officials of different departments.
Just to bring the matter to the attention of the committee I should like to read a brief section from a letter written by Mr. Mulford, the clerk of the corporation of the township of Chilliwack, to Mr. Cruickshank, dated May 15, 1952. It is as follows:
I understand you are aware of the proposed scheme to define and construct a permanent channel for the Vedder river, between the Vedder canal and the Vedder crossing bridge. The interested parties to this scheme at the present time are the provincial government, district of Sumas and the township of Chilliwack.
In the past, the river between these points has been allowed to wander, eating away at the banks and causing periodic flooding. Also there is always the danger of the river jumping its banks and flooding that area between Sardis and the canal in the township, thereby severing the trans-Canada highway, or moving through Yarrow and thereby flooding Sumas municipality.
That is just part of that letter. As I have intimated, I have other communications under various dates with reference to this matter. On August 2 there is a letter signed by Mr. Cruickshank and directed to Mr. Mulford. It reads as follows:
Re: Vedder river project.
The latest that I have from the Minister of Public Works re the above is as follows:-

Order. I am going to ask the hon. member's co-operation. Engineering studies for the purpose of making provision against such calamities do.

I realize the hon. member for Fraser Valley will most likely point out to me that three or four items further on there is a specific item dealing with surveys and investigations in

the Fraser river basin, and I think the river he is now discussing comes within the Fraser river basin.
However, I take it the committee will not mind if I put the matter this way. I am not ruling the hon. member out of order. I am asking him to bear in mind the remarks I have made, and I would ask that if he and other members who have rivers within their jurisdictions consider it necessary to bring to the attention of the minister of the department the necessity for surveys or investigations in connection with possible flood control, they do so as briefly as possible.

The Department of Public Works might be given the duty of building protective works, but certainly it is not the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources which can accept liability for the federal authority, as has been done in previous cases in the Fraser valley and other places, as the result of calamity. speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is what the whole study is for, and that is why I was asking who the expert was who could say in advance what the result of the surveys will be. The surveys are for the purpose of indicating, among other things, if it is possible to divert the waters of the Columbia river into the Fraser river without endangering the fisheries of the Fraser river. They will indicate also if it is economically feasible and advantageous, but the first condition is that it does not harm the fisheries. That is exactly why these studies are going to be made, and that is why I was surprised to hear that somebody already had the answer before the surveys were made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Are you planning to discover whether you can divert the river before you discover whether or not the fish can make the grade up half a dozen dams on the Fraser river?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It is all part of the study, because the effect on the fish depends on the height and character of the dams and on the volume of water that might be diverted. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is why I am objecting to this particular expenditure, because you are now proposing to take water from the Columbia river to a particular spot up on the mountainside, and then divert it down into the Fraser, without knowing first whether or not the fish will live.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have to interrupt the hon. member because I did not say we were proposing to divert the waters of the Columbia to the Fraser. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, may I say we hope that by next year we shall know definitely whether a diversion is economically feasible under the conditions I just mentioned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

Seven thousand are in the Northwest Territories, and 2,000 are under the administration of this department in northern Quebec. They are dependent for subsistence very largely on caribou.
One of the things that was left incomplete in the committee was this. I was asking questions concerning the 2,000 Eskimos in the northern part of Quebec who at one time, according to Mr. Cunningham, who gave us most of the information on this problem, were in a relatively happy state as a hunting population because caribou were extensive. In recent years, however, the caribou have entirely disappeared, and further evidence brought out the fact that these particular Eskimos are being trained to become water hunters, which they were not before, and to hunt the seal and walrus.
It was mentioned that they do not have immediate adaptability and it is not easy to retrain them. I asked if that area of northern Quebec could be restocked with caribou. It was pointed out that this had been considered, but it was thought an extraordinarily slow process and that therefore other methods of providing for the livelihood of these people were being considered.
That is the point which I think was left incomplete. I wonder if the minister would take into consideration again the restocking of that area with caribou, even if it does take a long time. There has been considerable experience in Canada in, for example, the preservation of buffalo and elk. They are living in restricted areas, and as they multiply they keep up their numbers. There has also been considerable experience in developing reindeer herds. We were informed that the 800,000-odd caribou to the west of Hudson bay are sufficient to support the Eskimo population in that area who are dependent as hunters on caribou.
For the northern Quebec area, using the estimate we have been given, it would take perhaps 200,000 caribou to support the Eskimo families there, who require, we are told,

Supply-Northern Affairs between 70 and 100 caribou a year to give them sustenance. As I say, we have had experience in saving other types of wildlife, and in restocking. I read an article in a newspaper the other day, which may or may not be accurate, stating that moose had been non-existent in Newfoundland until they were taken there 55 years ago, but now, even with the hunting, the moose population has increased to 50,000.
Would it not be wise to reconsider introducing caribou into that particular area? The seal and walrus might fail; then we are left with the problem of simply providing subsistence for the native population. The reason the native population has been placed in these dire circumstances was brought out in the committee and I shall not go into it again now, but I simply ask the minister to reconsider this matter. Next year we shall put two or three questions to him and see what the answers are.
